seo_desc: Gout in the big toe or foot? Podiatrists in Jupiter and Palm Beach Gardens confirm the diagnosis, calm the flare and help prevent the next. (561) 915-1934
lede: A big toe that turns red, hot and too painful to touch overnight is often gout. Our podiatrists can confirm it and help calm the flare.
what_it_is: Gout is a type of inflammatory arthritis caused by uric acid that builds up and forms needle shaped crystals in a joint. Your body makes uric acid when it breaks down purines, which come from your own tissues and from foods such as red meat, organ meats, shellfish and beer. The American College of Foot and Ankle Surgeons explains that the big toe joint is hit most often because uric acid crystallizes more easily in cooler areas, and the toe is the coolest point, farthest from the heart.

According to NIAMS, gout is more common in men and usually appears in middle age, while women rarely develop it before menopause. High blood pressure, diabetes, obesity, kidney disease, a family history and certain medicines such as diuretics and low dose aspirin raise the risk. Gout tends to come in flares separated by quiet periods, and repeated flares can leave lasting joint damage, which is why it is worth treating even after a flare settles.
symptoms: Sudden, intense pain in the big toe joint, often starting at night or on waking
Redness and warmth over the joint
Swelling that can make a shoe or even a bed sheet hard to tolerate
Pain that can also strike the ankle, top of the foot or knee
Firm lumps under the skin (tophi) after years of repeated flares
causes: High uric acid levels from making too much or clearing too little
Diets rich in red meat, organ meats and shellfish, and drinks such as beer and sugar sweetened beverages
Being overweight, high blood pressure, diabetes or kidney disease
Diuretics, low dose aspirin, niacin and some other medicines

how_therapy_helps.intro: Treating gout has two goals: calming the current flare and lowering the chance of the next one. The American College of Foot and Ankle Surgeons notes that with treatment, symptoms of a gout attack typically resolve in three to ten days. Mayo Clinic describes prescription anti inflammatory medicines, colchicine and corticosteroids, taken by mouth or injected into the joint, for flares, and medicines that lower uric acid for people with repeated attacks. Confirming that a red, swollen toe is gout and not infection is the first step.
methods: Mayo Clinic notes that drawing a small amount of fluid from the joint to look for urate crystals, along with blood tests and imaging, can confirm gout and rule out infection or other causes.
Your podiatrist can prescribe anti inflammatory medicine or colchicine, which Mayo Clinic says works best within 24 hours of the start of symptoms.
Mayo Clinic notes that corticosteroids for a flare can be taken by mouth or given as a shot into the joint, and the ACFAS lists injections among initial treatments.
The ACFAS recommends keeping weight off the foot and elevating it during an attack to ease swelling and pain.
Drinking plenty of water and cutting back on purine rich foods, beer and sugary drinks are first line advice from the ACFAS and Mayo Clinic, and gradual weight loss can lower uric acid.
For repeated flares, medicines that lower uric acid are usually managed with your primary care doctor or a rheumatologist, and your podiatrist can coordinate that care.

first_visit: At your first visit the podiatrist asks when the pain started, how fast it came on, whether you have had attacks before, and about your diet, alcohol, medications and conditions like kidney disease. They examine the joint for redness, warmth, swelling and tophi, and check for fever or broken skin that could suggest infection. They may order blood work, imaging or a joint fluid test, then explain options for the flare and the next steps.
recovery: The American College of Foot and Ankle Surgeons notes that with treatment, the symptoms of a gout attack typically resolve in three to ten days. NIAMS describes flares that typically get better over a week or two, and Mayo Clinic notes lingering discomfort can last days to weeks. Without changes, flares often return and can come more often, and over years they can damage the joint or form tophi. NIAMS also notes that with early diagnosis, treatment and lifestyle changes, gout is one of the most controllable forms of arthritis.
self_care: Rest the foot and keep it elevated, and use a cool pack wrapped in a thin towel for short periods
Drink plenty of water and avoid alcohol, especially beer, during a flare
Skip red meat, organ meats, shellfish and sugar sweetened drinks for now
Do not start or stop prescription medicines on your own, and ask your doctor before taking aspirin for the pain
see_a_doctor: Fever or chills with a hot, swollen joint, which Mayo Clinic warns may mean infection and needs care right away
A first episode of sudden, severe joint pain, so the cause can be confirmed
Red streaks, an open sore or drainage near the swollen joint
Symptoms that are not improving after several days of treatment
Repeated attacks, or new firm lumps under the skin near a joint

faqs.q: Why does gout usually start in the big toe?
faqs.a: The American College of Foot and Ankle Surgeons explains that uric acid is sensitive to temperature, and the big toe is the coolest part of the body because it is the farthest from the heart. In cooler joints, uric acid is more likely to form crystals. NIAMS notes that many people have their first gout flare in one of their big toes.

faqs.q: How long does a gout attack in the foot last?
faqs.a: According to the American College of Foot and Ankle Surgeons, the symptoms of a gout attack typically resolve in three to ten days with treatment. NIAMS notes that flares usually last a week or two. Mayo Clinic describes pain peaking in the first 8 to 12 hours, then lingering discomfort that can last days to weeks, so starting treatment early helps.

Yes. Podiatrists are physicians who treat foot and ankle conditions, and gout most often strikes the big toe. A podiatrist can examine the joint, order tests to confirm gout and rule out infection, prescribe medicine for the flare and offer a joint injection when appropriate. For long term uric acid lowering, they often work alongside your primary care doctor or a rheumatologist.

Foods high in purines raise uric acid. The ACFAS and Mayo Clinic point to red meat, organ meats such as liver, shellfish and certain fish like anchovies and tuna. Beer, red wine and drinks sweetened with fructose are also common triggers. Drinking plenty of water helps, while cutting back on these foods lowers the odds of a flare.

faqs.q: Is it gout or an infection in my toe?
faqs.a: Both can cause a red, hot, swollen toe, which makes them hard to tell apart at home. Fever, chills, an open wound or red streaks spreading from the area raise concern for infection, and Mayo Clinic advises seeking care right away for fever with a hot, inflamed joint. A doctor can test fluid from the joint to tell the difference.

faqs.q: Can gout damage your foot permanently?
faqs.a: It can if flares keep returning over years. NIAMS describes a late stage where urate crystals build up into hard lumps called tophi, which can cause joint damage and deformity. Ongoing high uric acid is also linked to kidney stones. Treating flares promptly and lowering uric acid when attacks repeat helps protect the big toe joint.

notes_for_reviewer: Please confirm the doctors offer corticosteroid joint injections and joint aspiration for gout (not on the listed services). The ACFAS page refers to 'injections' generally.
The page says the podiatrist 'may order' blood work, imaging or joint fluid testing, since in-office lab or imaging is not a listed service. Confirm wording.
Long term uric acid lowering is framed as coordinated with primary care or rheumatology. Adjust if the doctors manage allopurinol or similar themselves.
ICD-10 M10.9 is 'Gout, unspecified' (verified, billable). More specific foot codes (for example idiopathic gout of the ankle and foot) were not verified and are not used.
Mayo Clinic describes pain peaking in the first 8 to 12 hours; NIAMS says flares last a week or two; ACFAS says 3 to 10 days with treatment. All three are attributed separately in the text.

Fact-check: the self-care tip to use a cool pack during a flare is not stated in the cited ACFAS, NIAMS or Mayo pages (ACFAS says rest and elevate). It was kept as conservative general advice; remove it if you prefer only sourced self-care.
